lesson.title: tc netem: Breaking the Network on Purpose
lesson.summary: tc netem is a Linux traffic-control tool that injects controlled delay, packet loss, and jitter into an interface, letting you test how software actually behaves under bad network conditions instead of guessing.
lesson.body:
Software that works perfectly on a fast, reliable office or lab network can fall apart the moment it meets a real-world link: a mobile connection with variable latency, a satellite hop with long round trips, a congested WAN with occasional loss. Discovering that in production, from user complaints, is expensive. The alternative is to reproduce those bad conditions deliberately, in a controlled environment, before shipping, and on Linux the tool for that is tc netem.

netem is a queueing discipline, one of the building blocks of Linux's tc, or traffic control, subsystem, that you attach to a network interface. Rather than passing packets straight through, it delays them, drops a percentage of them, reorders them, or adds random jitter to their timing, according to rules you specify. This is a direct, hands-on way to work with latency and packet loss, not as abstract definitions but as conditions you can dial up or down and observe the effect of.

A few concrete examples of what you can apply to an interface:

  tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 100ms 20ms distribution normal

adds 100ms of latency to every packet leaving eth0, varying randomly by about 20ms around that mean, which emulates jitter on a real link rather than perfectly uniform delay.

  tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem loss 5%

drops roughly 5 percent of outgoing packets at random, emulating packet loss.

  tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 100ms loss 2% reorder 25% 50%

combines delay, loss, and reordering in a single rule, closer to what a genuinely poor link looks like in practice. Removing all of this is a single command, tc qdisc del dev eth0 root, which restores normal behavior.

netem is usually applied to a specific interface, and this is exactly where network namespaces become useful rather than incidental: instead of degrading an entire physical machine's networking, which would also break your SSH session and every other process on it, you apply netem to the veth interface belonging to one namespace, or to the host-side end of that veth pair, so only the traffic to and from that one simulated host is affected while everything else on the machine runs normally. This lets you build a small lab, for example two namespaces connected through a Linux bridge, and degrade only the link to one of them to represent a remote client on a poor connection while the rest of the environment stays clean.

A realistic use of this: a team building a mobile sync client wants to know whether its retry and timeout logic actually works, not just in theory but under real degraded conditions, before shipping. They apply tc qdisc add dev veth-client root netem delay 500ms 100ms loss 3% inside the namespace representing the mobile client, simulating a slow, jittery, lossy connection, and then run the sync client against the server and watch what happens: does it back off and retry correctly, or does it hang forever, or crash on an unexpected timeout. Measuring the effect quantitatively is where the earlier tools tie back in directly: running iperf3 across the degraded link shows exactly how much the induced delay and loss reduce achievable throughput, since a longer round-trip time combined with any loss forces TCP to slow down and retransmit, and running tcpdump or Wireshark alongside the test lets you actually see the retransmissions, the delayed ACKs, and the reordered segments that netem is manufacturing, connecting packet capture, throughput measurement, and controlled network emulation into a single realistic testing workflow.
